spec_match.rationale: A practical migration angle that checks each URL's authority against the forbidden-host-code-point set directly (deliberately, so it gives the Chrome 157 answer on older builds — the note says so), honours the file:// space exemption, and its code-path panel correctly warns that %20-encoding a host is not a fix.

interactive.rationale: Textarea input, scan/sample/clear buttons, live tallies and a findings table with per-URL verdict, reason and a suggested correction; the sample scan auto-runs at load (observed: 8 scanned, 3 will break).

blurb_alignment.rationale: The index card promises pasting a list and getting back which URLs Chrome 157 rejects, why, and the corrected form, entirely in-page — all delivered.

edge_cases.rationale: Empty lists, no-authority lines, the file:// exemption and the %20-is-not-a-fix trap are handled, and tab/LF/CR are correctly excluded as stripped-before-parsing — but the check runs against the whole authority, so a space in the userinfo (https://user name@example.com/), which the spec percent-encodes rather than rejects, would be misreported as 'will break'.

references.rationale: See-also cites https://chromestatus.com/feature/5083335148437504 and the forbidden-host-code-point section.

conformance.rationale: The feature suite backs this page's claims and ran with the expected 6 pass / 2 fail pre-157 split on Chromium 141; partial only because of the suite's percent-encoded-space-in-host assertion flagged for a human on the host-parser critique — notably this page's own copy ('a hostname that does not exist... a different bug, not a fix') is the more defensible framing.

runtime_evidence.rationale: Headless Chromium 141 (cloud, no chrome-devtools-mcp): the load-time sample scan genuinely ran — console logged 'scanned 8 urls, 3 will break' and the screenshots show the tallies (8/3/5) and the full findings table with corrections like stagingserver.example.com — while paste-your-own-list flows are judged from wiring.

telemetry_health.rationale: showcaseTelemetry?.assert fires scan-complete with totals on every scan including the observed initial one; console carries only the page's labelled logs.

design_system.rationale: Layout, tallies and buttons follow the design system, but the emerald 'parses'/'Fine' text (~3.7-4.1:1 on stone/white) repeats the shared palette AA shortfall; the rose 'rejected' state passes.

accessibility.rationale: The textarea is labelled, the outcome narrative is an aria-live=polite output, tallies are a definition list, the findings table has a caption and header row, and verdicts are text ('rejected'/'parses') rather than colour alone.

mobile_desktop_parity.rationale: Verified at true 360px and 1280px: buttons and tallies stack, the four-column findings table compresses inside the viewport via overflow-wrap:anywhere, and there is no horizontal overflow or clipped control on either class.

openQuestions.title: Authority check misclassifies spaces in userinfo
openQuestions.detail: authorityOf() returns everything between :// and the first /?#, which includes userinfo and port. A space in userinfo (https://user name@example.com/path) is percent-encoded by the URL parser, not rejected, yet the scanner reports it as 'the host contains a space — rejected'. Splitting the authority on the last @ (and the port colon) before checking, or cross-checking lines against new URL() when it agrees with the static analysis, would remove the false positive while keeping the deliberate gives-157-answers-on-old-builds design.

openQuestions.title: Space-deletion is presented as the correction without alternatives
openQuestions.detail: suggest() joins host fragments ('staging server' becomes 'stagingserver'), but the code-path panel itself lists three possible fixes (typo deletion, the space belonged in the path, it was really a file path). Showing the deletion as one candidate ('e.g. stagingserver... — or was this meant to be staging-server, or a path?') would stop the corrected column implying more certainty than the heuristic has. The Volumes/Users file:// rewrite is a nice touch and already does this properly.

summary: A genuinely useful migration tool with an unusually honest design decision: it checks the forbidden-code-point set statically so it reports the Chrome 157 verdict even on older builds — which this session confirmed, the sample auto-scan on Chromium 141 reporting '3 of 8 will be rejected' with correct per-line reasons (space hosts flagged; space-in-path, file://, query-space and %20 lines passed). Verified with headless Chromium 141 at http://localhost:3000/v157/disallow-spaces-in-non-file-url-hosts/migration-scanner/ (cloud, no chrome-devtools-mcp; desktop + true-360 mobile screenshots showing tallies 8/3/5 and the findings table, DOM dump, clean console; feature /conformance/ route 6 pass / 2 fail as expected pre-157). Two refinements: the authority check false-positives on userinfo spaces, and the corrected column could admit its heuristic nature.
